column6: The commentary says one admonition becomes beneficial only in its receiver; Hebrews says the good news reached the wilderness generation too, but the heard word did not benefit them because it was not joined with faith.
The fearful recipient of the reminder is set against the one who shuns it; Proverbs makes fear of YHWH the beginning of knowledge and says fools despise wisdom and discipline.
The page pictures deliberate sidelining rather than panic flight; Zechariah's ancestors refuse to heed, turn a stubborn shoulder, and stop their ears against prophetic correction.
Zechariah says they made their heart hard lest they hear Torah and the former prophetic words sent by the Spirit, identifying the offence as rejecting a word that has actually arrived.
God sets out ancient paths in which rest could be found, but the people answer that they will not walk there; this closely matches the offered guidance and chosen refusal in the commentary.
Instead of inclining their ear, people walk after their own counsel and stubborn heart and go backward; it makes self-directed turning from the reminder an alternative course, not a lack of access.

Ezekiel warns the wicked to turn; if the listener does not turn, he dies in iniquity while the watchman has discharged his task. This closely frames the commentary's non-coercive admonisher and responsible hearer.
The audience hears Ezekiel's words as a pleasant song but does not do them; this is a concrete counterpart to advice kept beside oneself rather than taken inward.
Wisdom's call and extended hand are refused, providing a particular scene of one offered instruction being rejected.
Those addressed neglect all counsel and refuse reproof, an exact ethical reversal of taking a beneficial reminder.
The liturgical call to hear God's voice today makes hearing a present response to divine address, closely framing the split between receiving and avoiding the reminder.
After the call to hear, the worshiper is told not to harden the heart as at Meribah; it gives the commentary's inward resistance a concrete historical and liturgical form.
Hebrews tells hearers to pay much closer attention to what they heard lest they drift away, capturing the page's quiet, continuing movement of putting admonition to one side.
Paul says opponents thrust the word of God aside and thereby judge themselves unworthy of eternal life; the self-directed rejection and outcome closely match the ashqa's active avoidance.
James calls those who hear the word without doing it self-deceived, sharpening the commentary's claim that the issue is what a person does with unchanged counsel.
James contrasts the forgetful hearer with the doer who remains at the perfect law and is blessed, directly accompanying the commentary's identification of turning from signs with forgetting them.
Paul's one ministry is an aroma among those being saved and those perishing; the shared proclamation yielding divided hearers mirrors the commentary's single reminder.

column5: death to death, life to life
column6: The one aroma becomes death to death for some and life to life for others, supplying a compact Christian form of the page's same word and opposed destiny pattern.
The word of the cross is folly to those perishing but God's power to those being saved, another specific instance of one preached message differently received.
Jesus addresses people who search Scripture yet are unwilling to come to him for life; it connects proximity to revealed words with an active refusal of their life-giving offer.
People turn their hearing away from truth and turn toward myths; this gives the page's turning from remembrance a particular alternative object.
Ezekiel's rebellious house has eyes to see and ears to hear yet does neither, directly illuminating the page's post-refusal blindness as a moral response to signs rather than lack of organs.
YHWH's servant sees much but does not observe and has open ears but does not hear, adding a prophetic image for instruction available yet spiritually unreceived.

The self-satisfied speaker claims to need nothing but is called wretched, poor, blind, and naked. These terms concentrate the page's self-sufficiency, wretchedness, judgmental blindness, and Edenic exposure.

column5: do not forget what was seen
column6: Moses tells Israel to guard itself lest it forget what it has seen and to transmit it, a direct Torah counterpart to the commentary's moral reading of forgotten signs.
Moses warns Israel not to forget YHWH by failing to keep commandments, making forgetting an enacted refusal as the page does.
Israel quickly turns aside from the commanded way to make and worship a calf; it is a concrete biblical inversion of the commentary's contrast between shunning idols and shunning God's reminder.

column5: do not turn aside after non-profit
column6: Samuel forbids turning aside after empty things that cannot profit or deliver; the page reverses this relation when the wretched treats beneficial admonition as the thing to avoid.
Israel is warned lest the heart be deceived so that it turns aside to serve other gods, supplying the inward deception behind the inversion of proper avoidance.
Paul asks believers to cleanse themselves from every defilement and complete holiness in fear of God, closely joining self-work, purification, and fear as the commentary joins them.
Everyone whose hope is fixed on him purifies himself; the active reflexive act is a direct Christian analogue for the commentary's account of tazakka as work done on oneself.

In Genesis the ground is cursed and eating becomes toil because the command was disobeyed. The page's post-garden hunger and hardship belongs beside this account, while its differently specified privations remain meaningful.
Genesis defines post-garden hardship as bread by sweat until return to dust; the page sets this mortal toil-and-death frame beside its later fire in which one neither dies nor lives.
Joshua says Terah and Abraham's ancestors served other gods beyond the River; the page turns that family background into Abraham's explicit anti-idol admonition and withdrawal.

Genesis Rabbah has Abraham expose the powerlessness of Terah's idols, a Jewish interpretive counterpart to the page's Abraham asking his father why he worships things that cannot hear, see, or help before separating from them.
Pharaoh's refusal to obey YHWH in response to Moses supplies the Hebrew Bible scene behind the page's Moses invitation to purification and Pharaoh's denial and turning away.

Isaiah's rebels are displayed where the worm does not die and fire is not quenched, giving a Hebrew Bible image of enduring punitive fire beside the great fire and non-ending condition developed on the page.
Jesus cites the undying worm and unquenched fire, closely paralleling the page's fate of entering great fire without death or life.
Jesus's final separation sends some to eternal punishment and the righteous to eternal life, supplying the page's polarized ultimate consequences in a judgment scene.
The smoke of idol-worshipers' torment rises for ages and they have no rest day or night, a specifically relentless Christian image for the commentary's prolonged, unrelieved fire.
Jesus asks what profit lies in gaining the whole world while forfeiting life; it mirrors the page's claim that the shunner substitutes worldly life for a beneficial reminder and loses lasting good.
The world and its desire pass away whereas the one doing God's will remains forever, directly accompanying the commentary's contrast of preferred worldly life with a better, more lasting hereafter.
God's kindness is meant to lead a person to repentance even when it is despised; this illuminates Moses's gentle invitation to Pharaoh to purify himself and the subsequent refusal.
Hebrews reads the Psalm's today as a mandate for daily mutual exhortation so none is hardened by sin's deceit, making sustained reminder a guard against the refusal described on the page.

The page calls final blindness a response to signs forgotten; Avot treats forgetting even one learned word as spiritually grave while distinguishing involuntary difficulty, sharpening the moral rather than merely mnemonic sense of forgetting.
God promises to cleanse Israel from uncleanness and idols; beside Abraham's plea to be kept from idols and the purified person in the page, it foregrounds divine protection as well as human response.
Draw near to God, cleanse hands, and purify hearts joins nearness and self-purification, helping the page's spatial language of the side and its call to purification read together.

column5: rising before dawn, hope in word
column6: The psalmist rises before dawn, cries for help, and hopes in God's word; it gives a particular biblical night posture joining departure from bed, prayer, and receptive hope rather than avoidance.
Walking with the wise makes one wise while companionship with fools brings harm, lending moral force to the page's companion and alien-neighbor reading of what stands at a person's side.

column5: good or evil friend and neighbor
column6: Rabbi Yohanan's disciples name good friend and good neighbor as ways of good, and evil friend or neighbor as ways to avoid; this gives a rabbinic companion reading for the page's side as either guide or estranged neighbor.

column5: life and good, death and evil
column6: Moses sets before Israel life and good versus death and evil, giving the page's extremes of ease and wretchedness a covenantal two-way framework.
Jesus's broad way leads to destruction and many enter it; the page's road image creates a specific comparison with an easy-seeming route terminating in ruin.
Jesus calls the way leading to life narrow and hard and says few find it, creating an illuminating tension with the commentary's easy way and hard ascent.
Baruch calls Israel to hear commandments of life and learn wisdom, a deliberate address to the hearing recipient that fits the page's reminder received by one person and avoided by another.

column5: walking God's way and enduring peace
column6: Baruch says that walking in God's way would mean living in peace forever, closely paralleling the page's Adam passage where following divine guidance prevents wandering and wretchedness.

Genesis says the garden pair are naked yet unashamed, whereas the page's Qur'anic Adam passage defines Eden by absence of nakedness. The difference matters because the commentary treats nakedness as a concrete index of hardship.
Pharaoh's heart is hardened and he does not listen to Moses and Aaron; set beside the page's emphasis on self-initiated avoidance, this biblical hardening language makes a relevant agency difference.

column5: lake of fire as second death
column6: Revelation calls the lake of fire the second death, while the page insists its fire's inhabitant neither dies nor lives; the different death language creates a careful counter-reading of final punishment.
Abraham tells the rich man's brothers to hear Moses and the prophets; the page invokes Abraham and Moses around a warning that proximity to revelation does not compel reception.
